green.alt: Pre-flower colony of Common Milkweed showing upright stems with broad oval grayish-green opposite leaves and prominent pale midribs

fruit.alt: Cluster of large warty, spiny green teardrop-shaped Common Milkweed seedpods on a living plant with broad oval opposite leaves

dormant.alt: Split-open brown Common Milkweed seedpod still clinging to a dried winter stalk, encased in clear ice with hanging icicles against blue sky
dormant.credit: Anna Weyers / USFWS Midwest, Public Domain

maturity.years: Rarely blooms year 1 from seed (root focus); flowers year 2-3; full 3-5 ft and aggressive colony spread by year 3-4
maturity.notes: Has both a taproot and spreading rhizomes, so site it once where colony expansion is welcome, since it's hard to remove and will travel.

fallColor: seed heads feed goldfinches; stems persist
notes: Sunflower-yellow daisies for 2-3 months, earlier and longer than true Helianthus. Reliable, drought-tolerant, deer-resistant.

bloom.alt: Single yellow Heliopsis flower with conical golden disk and narrow rays in prairie

winter.alt: Dense standing colony of pale-tan dried Heliopsis stalks with persistent conical seedheads in late-fall meadow

maturity.notes: Year 1 from seed is a low rosette of opposite, toothed leaves with little or no bloom. Year 2 sends up branched 3-4 ft stems with the first reliable flush of golden daisies and conical centers from June onward. By year 3 the clump reaches full 3-5 ft height with a long Jun-Sep bloom and slowly widens into a long-lived perennial. Good to know: stems flop in rich, moist soil. Site it in average-to-lean ground in full sun and it will stay upright without staking.

fallColor: flat seed heads weather to brown
notes: Flat pearl-white flower heads carry for 3+ months above leathery dark-green basal foliage. Tough, drought-tolerant, deer-resistant; specialist for several native bees.

bloom.alt: Wild Quinine in bloom: flat-topped clusters of many small pearl-white popcorn-button flower heads held above rough, coarsely toothed dark-green leaves on hairy stems

green.alt: Upright Wild Quinine stems showing the rough, coarsely toothed lance-shaped dark-green leaves, with the first flat white flower clusters just opening at the stem tips

maturity.years: Moderate; blooms reliably by year 2-3 from seed as the taproot establishes
maturity.notes: Long-lived, deep-taprooted prairie perennial. Very drought-tolerant once established and best left undisturbed (resents transplanting); thrives in lean, well-drained soil in full sun.

fallColor: basal rosette holds wine-tinted through winter
notes: Compact 1-2 ft beardtongue with hairy stems and pale-violet-to-white tubular flowers. Thrives on rocky, dry soil; foundation bee + hummingbird draw.

bloom.alt: Hairy Beardtongue in bloom on a limestone outcrop: slender reddish-purple hairy stems bearing small two-lipped tubular flowers, pale lavender-violet outside with white mouths

maturity.years: Blooms from year 2 (first year builds the root); short-lived (~3-5 yrs) but self-seeds in place
maturity.notes: Needs sharp drainage and lean, rocky, or sandy soil; wet, rich ground causes crown rot. Let some seed drop to keep a colony going; otherwise nearly care-free.

notes: 5-8 ft towers topped by flat clusters of rich violet-purple flowers that draw swallowtails. Cut by half in June for a stockier branched plant.

bloom.alt: Tall slender Tall Ironweed stem topped with a flat open branched cluster of small deep magenta-purple tufted flower heads with no outer petals, toothed lance-shaped leaves alternating along the stem visible below

winter.alt: Skyward shot of standing tan Vernonia gigantea stalks against blue sky with persistent rust-brown seedheads bearing fluffy white-tan pappus bristles

maturity.notes: Plugs spend the first year building a deep, paw-shaped mass of roots and underground stems and typically produce their first sparse late-summer flowers in year 2, reaching full 5-8 ft height by year 3.

fallColor: candelabra seed stalks stand into winter
notes: Rings of leaves up a 4-6 ft stem, topped by a candelabra of slender white flower spikes. The seed stalks stand through winter, so leave them.

bloom.alt: Whole-plant Culver's Root bloom: multiple branched candelabra-shaped slender white spires radiating from a single base, protruding pollen-bearing threads giving the characteristic feathery look, the candelabra shape that rules out single-spike lookalikes.

maturity.notes: Year 1: low foliage clump establishing fibrous roots; Year 2: first candelabra spikes at partial height; Year 3: full 3-6 ft clump with peak whorled-leaf, branched-spike display; keep consistently moist the first two seasons and pinch stems by 1/3 in late spring if you want a shorter, bushier, less floppy plant.

fallColor: dried stems stand tan through winter
notes: Slightly larger and damper-loving than slender mountain mint; same white flower clusters that draw many pollinators. Mint-scented, deer-resistant, spreads by rhizome.

bloom.alt: Flat-topped clusters of many tiny white two-lipped flowers with faint purple spots, framed by narrow, lance-shaped leaves

green.alt: Upright square stems with narrow lance-linear opposite leaves and hairy stem angles, small flat-topped white flower clusters at the tips

maturity.notes: Blooms year 2-3 from seed (sooner from divisions); spreads by rhizome into colonies. Likes moist to average soil; draws many pollinators, and the mint scent keeps deer away.

fallColor: airy yellow plumes along zig-zag stems; seed heads persist
notes: The only goldenrod for shade: 1-3 ft with zig-zag stems and small yellow flower clusters where the leaves meet the stem. A key late-season pollinator plant for woodland edges where most goldenrods can't grow.

bloom.alt: Broad egg-shaped, sharply toothed leaves framing small rounded yellow flower clusters tucked where the leaves meet the stem along its length, the bloom habit of zigzag goldenrod, not a plume at the stem tip

winter.alt: Standing plant with fluffy white spent seed clusters where the leaves meet the stem and broad toothed leaves partly yellowing, in woodland leaf litter

maturity.notes: Blooms Aug-Oct, year 2-3 from seed; spreads slowly by rhizome into loose colonies. Thrives in sun to full shade and moist woodland soil. Does not naturalize aggressively like field goldenrods.

fallColor: arching plumes of tiny yellow flowers; tan winter seed heads
notes: 3-5 ft goldenrod with arching horizontal sprays of bright yellow flowers in late summer. Tolerates wet feet better than most goldenrods, and gives nectar late in the season. Spreads by rhizome, so it is best in larger plantings.

bloom.alt: Arching, one-sided, horizontally radiating bright-yellow flower sprays curving outward from a central upright stem, forming the distinctive pyramidal plume of rough goldenrod

dormant.alt: Overwintering basal rosette of dark green wrinkled rugose leaves with deeply impressed veins and toothed edges lying flat among pine needles and leaf litter

maturity.notes: Blooms Aug-Oct, often the first full season from transplant. Spreads aggressively by rhizome, so site it in larger plantings or divide it. Tolerates wet soil; good for rain gardens and a source of nectar late in the season.

fallColor: fronds collapse with first frost; dark spore stalks persist
notes: Easy spreading wetland fern. Pale-green deeply-lobed fronds collapse at first frost (hence 'sensitive'), but stiff dark bead-like spore stalks persist erect through winter.

green.alt: Single pale-green Sensitive Fern sterile frond with winged-rachis pinnatifid blade and wavy-margined pinnae

maturity.notes: Year 1 sends up just a few isolated pale-green sterile fronds 8-12 inches tall from a small rhizome. Year 2 the rhizome network thickens and fronds reach near-full 1-2 ft size, with the first brown bead-like fronds that carry its spores appearing in late summer and persisting upright through winter. By year 3 it's running and forming a visible patch. In moist ground it spreads fast by underground stems. Plant it where you want a groundcover sweep, or sink a root barrier (or site it between hard edges) if you want to keep it contained. The sterile fronds collapse at the first frost, which is normal.

fallColor: yellow-green; dried flower domes hold into winter
notes: Wild form of 'Annabelle', with flat lacecap-domed white flower clusters for months. Cut to the ground in late winter for vigorous new wood and bigger blooms.

bloom.alt: Wild Smooth Hydrangea in bloom: a loose flat-topped to softly domed creamy-white lacecap cluster of small flowers ringed by a few larger ones, against heart-shaped, sharply-toothed leaves in pairs (not the tight Annabelle mophead)

green.alt: Smooth Hydrangea in late-spring leaf-out: a young shrub showing the paired arrangement of broad egg-shaped to heart-shaped, sharply toothed bright-green leaves on slender upright stems before flower buds open

fall.alt: Smooth Hydrangea in mid-October: yellowing toothed egg-shaped leaves still attached to the shrub in cream-to-yellow-green fall color, with a lingering dried maroon-brown flower dome at center

dormant.alt: Smooth Hydrangea in winter dormancy: leafless multi-stemmed loose colony with tan-cream papery domed seed heads still clinging to bare brown stems, glowing in low winter light

maturity.years: Fast (2-3 ft of new cane per yr); blooms on current-season wood the first summer after planting, reaches mature 3-5 ft mound in 2-3 yrs
maturity.notes: Blooms on new wood, so cut all stems back to 12-18 in. in late winter. Leaving the framework taller gives sturdier, smaller flower heads that don't flop in summer rain.

notes: Slender pink steeple-shaped flower clusters atop a 2-4 ft suckering shrub. Loves consistently moist to wet sites; fuzzy white undersides on the leaves.
Towering 4-8 ft tickseed with whorls of slender leaves and clouds of small yellow daisies into early fall. Surprisingly self-supporting; a bold plant for the back of a meadow planting.

fallColor: tan flower heads persist into winter
notes: Tallest of the Joe Pye Weeds at 5-7 ft, with a hollow purple-spotted stem, whorled leaves, and massive mauve-pink fuzzy flower domes. Draws butterflies to wet sites.

bloom.alt: Whole-plant Hollow Joe Pye Weed in bloom: tall stem topped with a domed mauve-pink flat cluster of fluffy flowers, with rings of narrow, pointed leaves at the lower joints along a pale unspotted stem.

green.alt: Non-flowering Hollow Joe Pye Weed with rings of 5 to 6 narrow, pointed leaves along the stem. Sweet Joe Pye Weed has 3 to 4 per ring.

maturity.years: Moderate; blooms first or second year from a quart pot (year 2 from seed), reaches mature 6-8 ft height by year 3 and ultimately 7-10 ft tall x 4-5 ft wide on rich moist sites
maturity.notes: Don't let it dry out the first two summers. The hollow stems and big leaves wilt fast on droughty ground, and chronic dry stress permanently stunts mature height. For a bushier 5-6 ft plant with later, more numerous (but smaller) flower heads, cut every stem back by one-third to one-half in late May or early June, just above a point where leaves join the stem.

notes: Towering 6-8 ft coneflower with deeply-cut leaves under drooping yellow ray petals around a green cone. The garden double 'Golden Glow' comes from this species; spreads by rhizome.

bloom.alt: Cutleaf Coneflower in bloom at the base of a tree: yellow daisy-like flowers with drooping or swept-back petals around the green-yellow raised central cone (not brown), with deeply 3 to 5 lobed leaves visible at the base.

green.alt: Spring emergence of Rudbeckia laciniata: a basal rosette of deeply 3-5 lobed pinnate 'torn' leaves spreading from reddish-pink emerging stems against bare soil in April.

dormant.alt: A roadside stand of Rudbeckia laciniata in January winter dormancy: multiple tall slender dried brown stems standing rooted in grass, each branched stalk tipped with persistent dried seed cones, against a leafless winter woodland in North Carolina.

maturity.years: Fast; first blooms in year 2 from a plug (year 2-3 from seed), reaches mature 5-9 ft height by year 3, then expands indefinitely into colonies via rhizomes and abundant self-sown seedlings
maturity.notes: In rich or moist soil the 6-9 ft stems will pancake in the first summer thunderstorm. Either cut all stems back by one-third to one-half in early-to-mid June for a shorter, sturdier, slightly later-blooming plant) or stake at 3 ft before flower buds form. Deadhead before seed shatters in fall if you don't want a self-sown thicket the following spring.

notes: Vigorous twining vine with foamy white star-flowers in late summer, then silky-plumed 'Old Man's Beard' seed heads. Needs a sturdy trellis or fence; cut hard in late winter.

bloom.alt: Virgin's Bower in late-summer bloom: cream-white flowers with four petal-like parts and green tufts of pollen-bearing threads on a twining vine, with the coarsely-toothed three-leaflet leaves visible (setting it apart from the invasive look-alike with smooth-edged leaves).

green.alt: Virgin's Bower foliage: a slender twining stem displaying paired leaves of three leaflets each, with coarsely toothed edges, the wiry purple-tinged stem looping around grass to climb.

fall.alt: Clematis virginiana in early October: dense billowing masses of silvery-grey plumose seed heads ('Old Man's Beard') draped over a hedgerow shrub, the long feathery persistent styles giving the vine a smoky frosted look.

maturity.years: Very fast; produces 10-20 ft of new vine per growing season once established (year 2+), first blooms in year 2 on new wood, reaches mature 15-20 ft length by year 3 and keeps that scale annually from the cut-back base
maturity.notes: It flowers on the current year's growth. Every February or early March, cut the entire vine down to 8-12 in. above the ground before buds break, otherwise you'll end up with a bare-bottomed tangle of brittle old stems with flowers only at the top. Give it a sturdy 8-10 ft trellis or chain-link fence (not a delicate obelisk), because the twining leaf stalks will smother small shrubs and saplings within a season.

notes: A well-known spring woodland flower. A hooded green-and-purple-striped 'pulpit' surrounds 'Jack', the upright spike in the middle. Goes summer-dormant; sets a cluster of glossy red berries in fall.

bloom.alt: Jack-in-the-Pulpit hood: striped green and dark purple hooded pulpit enclosing the club-shaped tip of the central spike, with leaves divided into three leaflets visible behind

green.alt: Two clear trifoliate Arisaema triphyllum leaves with prominent venation on a damp forest floor with fern fronds, post-bloom foliage stage

fruit.alt: Erect Arisaema triphyllum stem with a trifoliate leaf at the top and a bright red mid-stem cluster of ripening berries in summer woodland habitat

maturity.years: Very slow from seed (~2 yrs to germinate, ~5+ more to flower); divisions of the bulb-like root (corm) flower in 1-2 yrs
maturity.notes: Plants change sex with size: plants with a small bulb-like root (corm) are male, and only plants with a large, well-fed one produce the female pulpit and berries.

notes: Kidney-shaped fuzzy leaves form a slow-spreading mat; quirky red-brown jug-shaped flowers hide at ground level. Rhizomes have a true ginger scent (not edible).

bloom.alt: Wild Ginger flower at ground level: the 3-lobed maroon-brown jug-shaped flower hidden among leaf litter, with a hairy leaf stalk rising above and curling petal-like tips flush with the soil.

green.alt: Top-down view of a Wild Ginger colony at Mount Airy Forest, Cincinnati: paired matte-green heart or kidney-shaped leaves with prominent veining and smooth edges, a maroon flower bud just visible at ground level.
green.credit: Chris S. Packard / Earthdirt, CC BY 2.5

maturity.years: Slow; settles in during year 1 with little visible growth, begins spreading 6-8 in. per year by underground stems from year 2 onward, knits into a solid groundcover carpet by year 3-4 when plugs are set 12 in. apart
maturity.notes: Transplant or divide only in early spring just as leaves unfurl (or in early fall). The shallow horizontal rhizomes resent disturbance during summer heat and the plant will skip a year of growth. Site it in consistently moist, humus-rich shade; even short droughts trigger leaf yellowing and dieback, and it will not rebound to fill gaps until the next spring.

fallColor: dark cones persist as goldfinch food
notes: A dependable black-eyed susan: a long-lived perennial (unlike Rudbeckia hirta, which lives about two years) with golden-yellow daisies for 3+ months. 'Goldsturm' is the popular selection from this species.

bloom.alt: Dense profuse 'Goldsturm' Rudbeckia fulgida clump with golden-yellow rays and dark central cones forming a thick perennial mass backed by Miscanthus 'Morning Light'

dormant.alt: January dormant state: low ring of overwintering egg-shaped leaves at ground level with last year's dried dark seed-cone visible to the side, surrounded by leaf litter and snow patches

maturity.years: Fast; quart/gallon plants reach full 2-3 ft size and bloom the first season, full clump by year 2
maturity.notes: Spreads by underground stems; divide every 3-4 yrs to keep clumps vigorous and prevent center die-out.

notes: Crimson tube-shaped flowers on 2-4 ft stems that draw hummingbirds. Long taproot prefers lean, well-drained soil; pairs well with little bluestem.

fallColor: one-sided yellow plumes over soft gray-green foliage
notes: Compact 1-2 ft goldenrod with gracefully arching one-sided plumes and soft gray-green leaves. Adapted to lean dry soil, so it won't flop or run like its larger cousins.

fallColor: sky-blue daisies over smooth blue-green stems
notes: Glossy blue-green clasping foliage on 2-4 ft stems, topped in fall with sky-blue daisies. The cleanest aster, and it rarely mildews. Pairs with little bluestem and goldenrod for the classic fall trio.

fallColor: frothy white flower domes over dark green leaves
notes: 3-5 ft woodland-edge perennial with airy white flower domes lighting up dry shade in late summer. Toxic to livestock (the historic 'milk sickness' culprit) but a source of late nectar in shade gardens.
Often dismissed as a weed of abandoned fields, but its copper-orange fall color and silver winter tufts show well in large groups. Thrives in poor, dry soil.
Wet-meadow sedge that grows in dense clumps, with bristly foxtail-like seed heads. Grows well in stormwater ponds, rain gardens, and along streams; tolerates short flooding.

fallColor: tan blades; seed heads weather and drop early
notes: A grass that greens up early and goes semi-dormant in summer heat. Big nodding bristly wheat-like seed heads. Grows fast from seed, so it shelters slower plants in a seed mix.

fallColor: golden to red (depends on the variety)
notes: Adaptable grass that grows in summer heat, with narrow upright clumps and open airy seed-head clouds. Tolerates wet to dry; named varieties vary widely in height and fall color.

green.alt: Close view of upright blue-green narrow switchgrass blades (cultivar 'Cloud Nine') in summer growth, with emerging flower-cluster stems

bloom.alt: Switchgrass clump in full bloom showing the open, airy branched flower cluster of tiny pinkish-purple flower spikes above leafy stems

fall.alt: Whole switchgrass clump ('Shenandoah') in autumn, foliage turned vivid golden-yellow to bronze-gold in a landscape bed

maturity.years: Medium-fast from plug; sends up new shoots within ~6 wks, blooms year 1, full height & clump by year 2-3
maturity.notes: Seed stands are weed-prone in year 1, so start from plugs and keep competition down until established.

notes: Tallgrass-prairie companion to big bluestem, with narrow upright clumps and shimmering coppery-gold plume seed heads. Looks best with morning or evening sun behind it.

winter.alt: Backlit frost crystals on dried compact golden-bronze Indian grass plumes at sunrise: winter prairie scene

dormant.alt: Two upright dormant Indian grass plumes standing tall over a tan dried-prairie clump under blue sky in late March: pre-burn standing seedhead silhouettes

green.alt: Strongly blue-gray upright Indian grass clump of long narrow blades with a waxy coating, late June

bloom.alt: Multiple tall upright Indian grass stems each topped with a single compact golden-bronze plume catching warm light against meadow background

fall.alt: Clump of fall Indian grass showing multiple persistent bronze-brown compact plumes amid tawny straw-colored fall foliage, early November

maturity.years: Typical pace for a summer-growing grass: little top growth in year 1, more in year 2, a big jump in year 3, full 4-7 ft bloom stalks by year 3
maturity.notes: Needs hot sun, patience, and tall neighbors to lean on, or it flops once it finally bolts.

fallColor: dark seed cones feed goldfinches into winter
notes: Drooping pale-rose petals around a dark cone. Blooms slightly earlier and looks more delicate than Purple Coneflower. Best in dry well-drained soil; range stops just shy of KY.

bloom.alt: Single Pale Purple Coneflower head with very long narrow drooping pale-pink ray petals and a dark coppery-brown central cone against a prairie horizon

green.alt: Dense prairie colony of Pale Purple Coneflower showing the 2-3 ft unbranched stems topped with pale-pink drooping-rayed coneflower heads and narrow lance-shaped foliage

dormant.alt: Frost-coated Pale Purple Coneflower seed heads on bare stems standing in a dormant winter prairie in soft cool-toned light

maturity.years: Moderate; first sparse bloom in year 2 from seed, full 2-3 ft flowering clump by year 3, long-lived (10+ yrs) once the taproot is down
maturity.notes: Forms a single deep taproot rather than a fibrous crown, so it neither divides nor transplants well. Leave it in place and let it self-sow to make more.

fallColor: tan seed heads stand into winter
notes: Opposite leaves fuse around the stem (perfoliate) under flat-topped white flower clusters. Wet-meadow native, beloved by small native bees and wasps.

bloom.alt: Whole-plant Boneset with flat-topped fuzzy white flower clusters above paired leaves that join around the stem

green.alt: Whole-plant Boneset showing the paired leaves that join around the stem: the stem piercing fused single leaves at successive joints

winter.alt: Standing dead Boneset stalks with lingering dried leaves joined around the stem and fluffy white-tan seedheads in pine forest
winter.credit: Scott Allen Davis (iNat milkweed_mapper), CC BY 4.0

maturity.notes: Year 1 is a low rosette of those paired leaves that wrap around the stem, maybe 12-18" tall, often with a single small flowering stem late in the season. Year 2 hits 3-4 ft with the full fuzzy white flat-topped bloom heads in August-September, and by year 3 the clump is 3-5 ft tall and wide and at peak pollinator value. Don't site it where the soil dries out hard in midsummer. It tolerates clay and standing water but will collapse and look terrible during a drought in lean, dry soil.

notes: Tall airy prairie native with a gray-brown cone surrounded by long drooping bright-yellow petals. Crushed seed heads release an anise scent; goldfinch food in fall.

bloom.alt: Multiple Ratibida flowers against blue sky with drooping yellow rays and tall cylindrical brown cones

dormant.alt: Standing-in-place Ratibida stalks with persistent dark cylindrical bare cones in front of frozen pond

maturity.notes: Year 1 is a basal rosette of deeply pinnate, anise-scented leaves with no bloom. Year 2 typically throws a few wiry 3-4 ft stems carrying the first drooping yellow rays around tall gray-brown cones. By year 3 the clump is full-sized at 3-5 ft with airy, see-through bloom from June into August and starts dropping seed nearby. Good to know: it self-sows heavily. Leave the cones standing and you'll get a free colony, or deadhead in fall if you want to keep it in bounds.

notes: Tallgrass-prairie icon with deeply lobed 12+ inch basal leaves that align north-south to manage midday sun. Long-lived 15+ ft taproot, so site it permanently. Lemon-yellow sunflower-like heads on towering 6-10 ft stalks.

bloom.alt: Whole-plant Compass Plant at the U.S. National Arboretum in July: a single tall stalk on the left bears an alternating spike of large yellow sunflower heads against open sky, with shorter plants and the Capitol columns in midground.

green.alt: Compass Plant leaf portrait: large oak-like leaves at the base, cut nearly to the central vein into 5 to 9 sharp lobes.

maturity.notes: Year 1: small rosette of deeply cut basal leaves while taproot drives 6+ ft down; Year 2: larger rosette, rarely blooms; Year 3-4: first flowering stalk, often partial height; Year 5: full 6-10 ft bloom stalk; site it permanently on first planting, because the deep taproot makes mature plants impossible to transplant.

notes: Candelabra of slender 3-6 ft stems topped with pencil-like purple-blue flower spikes that bloom from the bottom up over months. Good for wet meadows, ditches, and rain gardens.
Classic 1-2 ft tickseed for dry sunny meadows, with golden-yellow daisies all early summer. Deadhead for extended bloom; self-sows freely in poor soil.

fallColor: sturdy sunflower heads age to bronze
notes: Like a shorter, better-behaved Compass Plant: 3-6 ft with stiff opposite leaves clasping the stem and clusters of lemon-yellow sunflower heads through mid-late summer. Self-supporting and long-lived.
4-6 ft mint family with pale yellow bottlebrush flower spikes for months. Tolerates more shade than other agastaches; dark seed spikes hold their shape through winter.

fallColor: feathery silver-green foliage holds through fall; flat seed heads
notes: Drought-tolerant 1-3 ft perennial with finely cut fernlike foliage and flat white flower clusters from late spring into summer. Tough lawn-alternative for sunny lean soil; spreads by rhizome to form mats.

green.alt: Whole-plant Yarrow with dense feathery fern-like finely-divided foliage at the base filling the frame and white flat-topped clusters at top.

bloom.alt: Pure white flat-topped flower cluster of wild-form Yarrow on a slender stem rising from a ring of feathery fern-like leaves at the base in a sunny meadow.

winter.alt: Yarrow in mid-November with a drying tan-cream flat-topped cluster on a slender stem and semi-evergreen feathery foliage at the base in a late-autumn meadow.

maturity.years: Fast; blooms first year from a quart pot (year 2 from seed), settles into a 2-3 ft tall x 2-3 ft wide clump by year 2-3, then expands outward via shallow rhizomes
maturity.notes: Plant in lean, unamended, well-drained soil with no compost or fertilizer added. Rich or irrigated ground produces tall, weak stems that flop open from the center by midsummer. Deadhead the first flush in early July (cutting back by half) to trigger a smaller second bloom in fall, and lift/divide every 2-3 years in early spring to discard the woody dying center before the clump opens up.

fallColor: clouds of true sky-blue daisies; arrow-shaped basal leaves
notes: 2-3 ft prairie aster with clouds of small sky-blue daisies in fall. Drought-tolerant once established; arrow-shaped leaves at its base give it interest before it blooms.

fallColor: violet to pale blue asters in September and October
notes: Large heart-shaped basal leaves form a weed-suppressing carpet under trees, sending up 1-3 ft stems of pale blue-white daisies in fall. A specialist for dry shade where most asters won't grow; spreads slowly to colonize.

fallColor: arching blue-purple stems with yellow flower clusters where each leaf meets the stem
notes: Refined 1-3 ft shade goldenrod with arching wand-like stems dusted blue-purple, with small yellow flower clusters where each leaf meets the stem (a wreath effect). A well-behaved goldenrod for woodland gardens; well-mannered and clumping.

fallColor: warm yellow in fall before dieback; bronze fronds that carry its spores
notes: Stately 2-5 ft fern with twice-pinnate, almost locust-like fronds and distinctive bronze fertile spikes at frond tips. The signature fern of seeps, stream banks, and wet woodlands.

green.alt: Royal Fern along a wet path edge showing the large twice-divided fronds with widely-spaced rectangular-oblong green leaflets resembling locust foliage.

fall.alt: Osmunda regalis in October in Dane County, Wisconsin, with fronds turned a uniform golden-russet fall color and characteristic widely-spaced rectangular-oblong leaflets visible.

maturity.years: Slow; reaches 2-3 ft fronds the first season after planting, full 3-4 ft (to 6 ft in wet shade) mature crown in 3-5 yrs, then builds a woody trunk-like base over decades
maturity.notes: Grows from a thick woody rhizome that hates being moved and may sulk a season or two after transplant. Set out container plants in early spring before the fiddleheads uncoil, keep the crown consistently wet the first year, and don't try to divide an established clump.

notes: Bold-leaved alumroot with fuzzy maple-shaped foliage holding through winter and airy white flower spikes in late summer. Tolerates poor rocky soil and is the best Heuchera for our humid summers.

fallColor: clear yellow fall color; persistent dark pods rattle in winter
notes: Kentucky's namesake tree, towering 60-80 ft with huge leaves divided into many small leaflets, late to leaf out, early to drop. Plants are male or female; females bear thick reddish-brown seed pods that rattle through winter. Very tolerant of city conditions, drought, and pollution.

green.alt: Whole Kentucky Coffeetree in fresh spring leaf at the Arnold Arboretum, a broad rounded crown of fine compound leaves on a single dark trunk, beside a park path under a blue sky

fall.alt: Yellow-transitioning Kentucky Coffee Tree leaflets on twice-divided leaves, with several lingering dark mature seed pods hanging in the canopy

maturity.years: Fast when young, slowing to moderate (~1-2 ft/yr); 60-75 yrs to mature size, female pods begin around 8-10 yrs
maturity.notes: Leafs out very late (late May) and drops early (Sept). The bare-branch look most of the year is normal, not dieback.

notes: Native shade tree grown for fall color: 30-50 ft with horizontal branches, turning scarlet-orange weeks before other trees. Migrating birds eat its small bluish fruit. Tolerates wet sites; very long-lived.

green.alt: Whole-tree summer crown of a mature Black Gum in full leaf, pyramidal-to-rounded form with dense green foliage against blue sky

fruit.alt: Close shot of a Black Gum branch with mature dark blue-black berries hanging on long stalks among leaves transitioning from green to early-fall red and purple
fruit.credit: Matthew C Perry / USGS, Public Domain

maturity.years: Slow (~1-1.5 ft/yr); ~12-15 ft in 10 yrs; mature 30-50 ft in 30-50 yrs; very long-lived
maturity.notes: Long taproot makes transplanting very difficult, so site it permanently and plant small, young stock. The fall color and wildlife value are worth the wait.

notes: A tree that grows under taller trees, best known for its smooth, sinewy 'muscled' gray bark. 20-30 ft with hop-like seed clusters and warm orange-red fall color. Tolerates wet feet and deep shade.

green.alt: Whole American Hornbeam in fresh spring leaf at the US Botanic Garden, an open, airy crown of small toothed leaves on a single smooth grey trunk, against a blue sky

dormant.alt: Leafless multi-stemmed American Hornbeam in early spring at Great Swamp NWR, New Jersey, showing the smooth grey muscular fluted trunks against bare understory woodland

maturity.years: Slow (~1 ft/yr, ~8-10 ft per decade); reaches mature 20-30 ft height and spread in 30-40 yrs
maturity.notes: Sparse, deep lateral roots make field-dug specimens hard to move, so buy container-grown stock and transplant in early spring before leaf-out, not fall.

fallColor: sweet orange fruit after first frost
notes: Native fruit tree with distinctive blocky 'alligator-skin' bark and bittersweet orange fruit that ripens after first frost. Plants are male or female: only females fruit, and they need a male nearby. Long taproot makes it hard to transplant once established.

bloom.alt: Small urn-shaped cream-yellow American Persimmon flowers arrayed along a twig with egg-shaped green leaves in late May

green.alt: Alternating dark-green egg-shaped to oval shiny American Persimmon leaves with smooth (untoothed) edges on a sunlit branch

fruit.alt: Cluster of ripe orange American Persimmon fruits ('Szukis' selection) hanging from branches among yellowing autumn leaves

maturity.years: Slow; 4-9 yrs to first fruit from seed (3 yrs grafted), 10+ yrs to full production, 30-50 yrs to mature size
maturity.notes: Plants are male or female, so you need one of each within ~50 ft for fruit; deep taproot makes transplanting hard, so plant young and site permanently.

fallColor: large palmate leaves drop early; smooth buckeye fruit fall
notes: Showy 10-20 ft small tree/large shrub with foot-long upright clusters of fire-red tubular flowers timed exactly for spring hummingbird migration. Drops leaves early (often August). Toxic seeds.

bloom.alt: Red Buckeye in spring bloom: fire-red erect tubular flowers in an upright branched cluster above leaves with leaflets fanning out from one point, on a multi-stem shrub

green.alt: Post-bloom summer Aesculus pavia foliage with palmate compound leaves and two developing buckeye fruits hanging from the branch

maturity.years: Medium; reaches 10-15 ft in ~10-15 yrs, blooms ~4-6 yrs from seed
maturity.notes: Goes summer-dormant by August-September, so site it behind later-emerging perennials so the gap isn't conspicuous.

fallColor: brilliant red-purple fall color; persistent black fruit into winter
notes: Tough adaptable 3-6 ft shrub with white spring flowers, glossy black fruit clusters that persist into winter, and brilliant red-purple fall foliage. Tolerates wet, dry, sun, and part shade.

bloom.alt: Flat-topped cluster of open white 5-petaled Black Chokeberry flowers with deep pink-magenta pollen sacs among glossy dark-green toothed leaves in late spring

fruit.alt: Flat-topped clusters of pea-sized glossy black Black Chokeberry fruits in late summer with glossy green leaves beginning to turn red

fall.alt: Whole-hedge view of Black Chokeberry in bright scarlet-red fall foliage against a grey October sky, showing the compact suckering shrub habit

maturity.years: Moderate; blooms and fruits in year 2-3, reaches mature 3-6 ft size in 5-7 yrs
maturity.notes: Suckers profusely into a colony, so give it room or edit runners; gets leggy with age, rejuvenate by cutting oldest stems to the ground.

notes: 6-10 ft suckering shrub with deep maroon-brown apple-scented flowers in late spring and aromatic crushed bark and leaves. Fragrance varies, so try to buy plants in bloom to select for scent.

bloom.alt: Close-up of two open Sweetshrub flowers showing the deep maroon-brown globe of many strap-like petals, nestled among glossy egg-shaped leaves in pairs
bloom.credit: Great Smoky Mountains National Park, CC BY-SA 4.0

green.alt: Close-up of Sweetshrub foliage: undivided, glossy, egg-shaped leaves in pairs with smooth edges and prominent veins

maturity.years: Moderate; first bloom in year 2-3 from a nursery plant, mature 6-10 ft rounded shrub in 5-7 yrs
maturity.notes: Fragrance varies wildly seedling-to-seedling from rich fruit-punch to nearly scentless, so buy it in bloom and sniff before you buy, or choose a named clone like 'Athens' or 'Michael Lindsey'.

fallColor: white fruit favored by migrating birds; purple-bronze fall color
notes: Tough thicket-forming 6-15 ft shrub with flat white flower clusters in early summer and white pea-sized fruit on red stems, a food source for migrating birds. Suckers aggressively; site where it can colonize freely.

fallColor: vivid red winter twigs glow against snow; purple fall foliage
notes: 6-9 ft suckering shrub grown for its electric red young twigs that blaze against winter snow. White flat-topped flowers, bluish-white berries, purple-red fall foliage. Prune oldest stems hard in spring to keep twig color brightest.

bloom.alt: Flat-topped cluster of small 4-petaled white flowers at a branch tip, surrounded by egg-shaped leaves in pairs with curved parallel veins and a reddish young stem.

green.alt: Whole-shrub summer habit of Cornus sericea: multi-stem suckering clump in full leaf in an open park-like setting.
green.credit: USDA-NRCS PLANTS Database (Jennifer Anderson), Public domain

fruit.alt: Cluster of porcelain-white berries on red stalks framed by egg-shaped leaves in pairs with strong curved parallel veins, which set it apart from a related dogwood with blue fruit.

fall.alt: Whole small-shrub Cornus sericea with foliage turned deep purple-red, upright multi-stem habit in dry prairie/meadow surround.
fall.credit: USDA-NRCS PLANTS Database (Jennifer Anderson), Public domain

winter.alt: Red-osier Dogwood winter shot: multi-stem clumps spreading by root shoots, with bare blood-red young stems against a bright snowfield.
winter.credit: USDA-NRCS PLANTS Database (Jennifer Anderson), Public domain

dormant.alt: March 27 dormant Cornus sericea: red-stemmed suckering colony along the Little Maple River in Sleepy Hollow State Park, Michigan: riparian creek and bare deciduous forest backdrop.

maturity.years: Fast (2-3 ft of new cane per yr); reaches mature 6-9 ft tall by 7-10 ft wide colony in 4-5 yrs, then continues to widen by suckers indefinitely
maturity.notes: Brightest red winter color is only on 1-3 yr old stems. Either remove the oldest 20-25% of canes at ground level each spring, or cut the whole shrub down to 6-8 in. every 2-3 yrs in late winter to force a flush of vivid new shoots.

fallColor: yellow-purple-red fall color; dangling male catkins through late winter
notes: Multi-stemmed 8-15 ft suckering shrub with showy dangling yellow male catkins through late winter and edible hazelnuts in fringed husks in late summer. Native squirrels harvest most nuts before humans. Variable but often vivid fall color.

bloom.alt: Bloom-phase American Hazelnut in March Memphis: two dangling yellow-green male catkins shedding pollen on a bare hairy twig, with two visible magenta-red female flower tips protruding from upper buds, both flower types captured in one frame.

green.alt: Whole-shrub Corylus americana in May leaf: a multi-stem suckering shrub with deep green foliage and vertical stems in open woodland, the 8-15 ft thicket habit.

fruit.alt: American Hazelnut cluster on the shrub: about 4 immature pink-blushed nuts nestled inside clearly fringed leafy husks, the fringed (not beaked) husk that sets it apart from the beaked hazelnut.

maturity.notes: Year 1-2: single-stem establishment, 1-3 ft of growth; Year 3-4: begins suckering into a multi-stem thicket and produces first catkins; Year 5-6: reliable nut production at 6-10 ft; plant two or more genetically distinct shrubs within 50 ft for cross-pollination, as a lone plant will set few nuts.

fallColor: yellow-green fall foliage; seed capsules split in autumn and persist all winter
notes: Compact 1-5 ft mounded shrub smothered for two months with showy yellow flowers featuring bursts of bright stamens. Adaptable, drought-tolerant, deer-resistant, with attractive shreddy peeling bark for winter interest.

fallColor: electric orange-scarlet fall color; upright crimson fruit cones persist
notes: Aggressive 15-25 ft suckering shrub/small tree with velvety antler-like branches, clusters of fuzzy crimson fruit that stand upright into winter, and bright orange-scarlet fall color. Site where it can colonize; not for tidy borders. Fruit makes tart 'sumac lemonade'.

bloom.alt: Bright yellow erect male flower clusters of Staghorn Sumac at branch tips with surrounding leaves made of many leaflets in early July

green.alt: Canopy of bright green pinnate compound Staghorn Sumac leaves (long lance-shaped leaflets, unwinged rachis) with persistent dark cones from the prior season

fruit.alt: Whole-shrub habit of Staghorn Sumac in late summer with multiple erect crimson cone-shaped fruit clusters at branch tips and green leaves made of many leaflets

fall.alt: Electric orange-scarlet pinnate Staghorn Sumac fall foliage with persistent dark crimson cones at branch tips against a bright blue sky

dormant.alt: Close-up of a bare Staghorn Sumac branch in early March showing the velvety 'antler-fuzz' bark texture and lingering buds

maturity.years: Rapid; mature 15-25 ft height in 5-10 yrs, colony spread is ongoing
maturity.notes: Original stems are short-lived (~15-20 yrs) and die back as suckers take over. Site it where colony spread is welcome, or install a deep root barrier.

fallColor: red rose hips persist into winter; red-purple fall color
notes: Low 2-4 ft suckering native rose with simple single pink flowers in early summer, glossy red hips that hold through winter, and warm red-purple fall foliage. Tougher and better-mannered than introduced roses; forms loose colonies.

6-12 ft suckering shrub with dinner-plate sized white flower clusters in June and edible purple-black fruit clusters in August. Does well where the ground gets wet from time to time; draws pollinators and birds. Wine, jelly, syrup uses (cooked only).

bloom.alt: Mature American elderberry shrub in bloom along a walking path in Fairfax County, Virginia, late May: multiple flat-topped creamy-white flower clusters scattered across dense foliage of leaves made of many leaflets

green.alt: Close-up of American elderberry leaves growing in pairs, each made of 5 to 7 egg-shaped to lance-shaped, finely toothed leaflets, fresh mid-summer green

fruit.alt: Drooping flat-topped clusters of American elderberry fruit ripening from green to purple-black on reddish pedicels against a blue sky, with pinnate foliage

fall.alt: Late-autumn yellow-to-bronze foliage of American elderberry along Stone Heather Drive in Fairfax County, Virginia, lit warmly against a late-season sky

maturity.years: Fast (3-6 ft/yr); first fruit on 2nd-year wood in year 2-3, full thicket size in 3-5 yrs
maturity.notes: Individual canes are short-lived and weak-wooded. Cut spent stems back hard each winter and let suckers replace them.

fallColor: blue-black fruit; reliable purple-red fall color
notes: Versatile 12-15 ft small tree/large shrub with flat-topped white flower clusters in spring, edible blue-black fruit, and reliable purple-red fall color. Tolerates sun to deep shade and wet to dry sites. Easy to grow.

bloom.alt: Multiple flat-topped white clusters of small 5-petaled flowers above egg-shaped finely-toothed plum-like leaves against blue sky.

green.alt: Whole 12-15 ft multi-stem Black Haw Viburnum in full green summer foliage with dense rounded crown.

fall.alt: Whole-shrub Black Haw Viburnum at a lake edge showing showy red-purple-orange fall color with autumn trees in the background.

maturity.years: Slow to moderate (~12-24 in./yr); first bloom in year 2-3 from a nursery plant, first fruit set year 3-4, mature 12-15 ft multi-stem shrub or 20 ft tree-form in 15-20 yrs
maturity.notes: A lone shrub mostly cannot pollinate itself: it will flower heavily but set almost no fruit. Plant at least two shrubs grown from different seeds (not divisions of the same plant) within ~50 ft to get the blue-black fruit that draws birds.

fallColor: glowing red fruit clusters persist into winter; brilliant red fall foliage
notes: Taller cousin of Black Chokeberry: a 6-10 ft upright shrub with white spring flowers, glossy red fruit clusters that persist into winter, and red fall foliage. Tolerates wet, dry, sun, and part shade.

bloom.alt: Flat-topped cluster of white Red Chokeberry flowers with pink-red pollen sacs

fruit.alt: Cluster of bright red Aronia arbutifolia pomes on a serrate-leaved branch

fall.alt: Red Chokeberry shrub with foliage turning red-purple while bright red berry clusters still hang

winter.alt: Bare Red Chokeberry twig bearing a flat-topped cluster of lingering bright red fruits (rules out winterberry holly, which bears berries singly where the leaves meet the twig)

dormant.alt: Bare gray-brown Red Chokeberry twig with a persistent deep-red pome cluster and tiny emerging leaf buds in late winter

maturity.notes: Year 1 looks like a thin 12-18" upright whip; by year 2 it's a 2-3 ft multi-stem shrub that often produces its first small cluster of white-pink flowers and a handful of red berries. Full 6-10 ft height, heavy fruit set, and the signature blazing red fall color all arrive in years 4-5 as the clump widens by basal shoots. The plant gets leggy and bare-bottomed if left alone. Once established, cut a third of the oldest canes to the ground every few years to keep it dense and fruitful.

notes: Multi-stemmed small tree with clouds of white spring blossoms, edible blueberry-like June fruit, and brilliant orange-red fall color. Smooth gray bark gives winter interest. Host plant for many butterflies and skippers.

green.alt: Smooth egg-shaped to oval mature Allegheny Serviceberry leaves with fine teeth and no hairs

fruit.alt: Loose clusters of small reddish-to-purplish-black Amelanchier laevis pomes ripening on a branch in June

fall.alt: Multi-stem Amelanchier laevis small-tree habit in late autumn with smooth gray bark and patchy yellow leaves still on the branches

maturity.years: Medium-fast (~1-2 ft/yr); reaches 15-20 ft in ~10-12 yrs, blooms and fruits ~3-5 yrs from a nursery plant
maturity.notes: Fairly short-lived (~30-50 yrs) and suckers into a multi-stem clump. Remove suckers if you want a single-trunk tree form.

notes: Cloud-like fleecy white flower clusters drape this 12-20 ft multi-stemmed tree in late spring. Plants are male or female; only females produce blue-black fruit. Slow grower, late to leaf out. Now susceptible to emerald ash borer.

bloom.alt: Fleecy drooping branched clusters of narrow strap-like pure-white petals draping from Fringe Tree branches in late spring bloom

green.alt: Young multi-stem Fringe Tree in full summer leaf showing undivided, egg-shaped to oval green leaves in pairs on slender trunks

fall.alt: Multi-stem Chionanthus virginicus small tree in autumn with clear yellow fall foliage on a leaf-littered lawn at Morris Arboretum

maturity.years: Slow (~6-10 in/yr); reaches 12-20 ft in ~20-25 yrs, blooms ~5-8 yrs from seed
maturity.notes: Resents root disturbance, so plant small stock and leave it undisturbed; plants are male or female, so buy one in bloom or in fruit if you want fruit.

fallColor: clear yellow fall color, then spidery yellow flowers Oct-Nov
notes: Multi-stemmed 15-25 ft understory tree with the unusual habit of blooming after the leaves drop: spidery clear-yellow flowers Oct-Nov when nothing else is in bloom. Clean yellow fall foliage.

bloom.alt: Witch hazel branch in late-fall bloom with yellow wavy strap-petal flowers and a persisting yellow autumn leaf still attached, the combination that identifies this species

fall.alt: Witch hazel branch with yellow strap-petal flowers and broad uneven-edged egg-shaped leaves turning yellow at the same time, the fall-bloom-with-leaves pairing unique to this species

green.alt: Summer witch hazel foliage showing broad egg-shaped leaves with scalloped wavy edges and leaf bases that are uneven from side to side, with green developing seed capsules

dormant.alt: Whole-plant multi-stem witch hazel small-tree habit in winter with branches dusted by heavy snow, irregular zig-zag branching visible

maturity.years: Medium (~1 ft/yr); reaches 15-20 ft in ~15-20 yrs, blooms ~6-8 yrs from seed
maturity.notes: Intolerant of drought during establishment, so mulch deeply and water through the first 2-3 summers.

notes: Suckering 10-20 ft small tree forming dense thickets cloaked in fragrant white flowers in early spring (before leafout). Edible 1-inch red-purple plums in August. Good for wildlife: caterpillars of many butterflies and moths feed on it, and birds nest in its dense cover.

bloom.alt: Bare reddish-brown American Plum twigs covered in paired clusters of white 5-petal flowers with pink centers

green.alt: Multi-trunked thicket-forming small Prunus americana in early-June leaf, with compact rounded crown

maturity.notes: Year 1 is a slender 2-3 ft whip with sparse branching; year 2 adds lateral branches and the first root suckers start popping up nearby. Expect the first scattered white spring blooms and a handful of plums in years 3-4, with a real thicket and meaningful fruit set by years 5-6 as suckers fill in around the parent. Plant at least two seedlings from different sources for cross-pollination. American plum mostly cannot pollinate itself, and a lone tree will bloom heavily but fruit poorly.

notes: Graceful 2-3 ft arching woodland perennial with alternate clasping leaves and a frothy plume of small white flowers at stem tips in late spring, followed by speckled ruby-red berries in fall.

green.alt: Spring-emergent Maianthemum racemosum shoots in tight cluster with unfurling leaves and characteristic purplish stem bases

bloom.alt: False Solomon's Seal bloom: frothy white plume at the tip of an arching unbranched stem with alternating clasping egg-shaped to lance-shaped leaves (what sets it apart from Solomon's Seal)

fruit.alt: Terminal cluster of speckled green-tinged-red Maianthemum racemosum unripe berries at the stem tip above broad alternating parallel-veined leaves on an arching stem

fall.alt: Late-October Maianthemum racemosum: whole arching stem with broad alternating leaves yellowing and a terminal cluster of ripe bright-red berries

maturity.years: Slow; single shoots year 1-2, full arching stems by year 3, slowly colonizing clump in ~5+ yrs
maturity.notes: Roots resent disturbance, so set out small divisions and leave them alone; seed-grown plants take 3-4 yrs to first bloom.

notes: Semi-evergreen groundcover for shade. Purple-tinged heart-shaped basal rosettes hold through winter, sending up 1-2 ft stems of bright yellow daisy clusters in spring. Spreads steadily by runners; tolerates wet feet.

Spring-ephemeral woodland colony of paired umbrella-like leaves on 1-1.5 ft stems; a single nodding waxy white flower hides beneath each pair, followed by a fleshy yellow 'apple'. Foliage yellows and dies back by midsummer, so pair it with later-emerging companions.

bloom.alt: Single waxy white Mayapple flower (~2 in) hanging beneath the canopy of deeply lobed parasol leaves, with an unopened bud visible alongside

green.alt: Dense woodland colony of Mayapple: a sea of upright umbrella-shaped deeply lobed parasol leaves carpeting the forest floor

maturity.years: Slow; seed-grown plants take ~5 yrs to flower (two-leaf stage required); rhizome divisions establish in 1-2 seasons and colonies expand a few inches per year
maturity.notes: Single-leaf stems never flower; only mature two-leaf stems bloom. Goes fully dormant by midsummer; interplant with later perennials.

fallColor: blue-black berries; clear yellow fall color
notes: Arching 2-4 ft woodland perennial with paired dangling greenish-white bells beneath the stems in late spring, followed by blue-black berries. Foliage turns clear yellow in fall. Spreads slowly into long-lived colonies.

bloom.alt: Solomon's Seal bloom: clusters of greenish-white tubular bells dangling from where the leaves meet an arching stem with plain green egg-shaped leaves (what sets it apart from False Solomon's Seal)

green.alt: Arching unbranched Solomon's Seal stem with alternating egg-shaped clasping plain-green leaves and immature green berries dangling from where the leaves meet the stem

fruit.alt: Whole Solomon's Seal arching stems with clusters of dark blue-black berries dangling from where the leaves meet the stem

maturity.years: Slow; single shoots year 1-2, full-height arching stems by year 3-4, gradual non-aggressive clump in 5-7 yrs
maturity.notes: Has underground stems but does not spread into a colony. Divisions may sit dormant a full year before sending up shoots, so don't assume failure.

notes: Dry-shade sibling of Golden Ragwort: thick spoon-shaped semi-evergreen rosettes with yellow daisy clusters on 1-2 ft stems in spring. Slowly spreads by runners; a good groundcover for dry shade, where Golden Ragwort would fail.

fallColor: towering yellow sunflower clusters; edible knobbly underground tubers
notes: Native perennial sunflower: 6-10 ft stems crowned with bright yellow blooms in fall, and edible knobbly underground tubers (the 'sunchoke'). Spreads aggressively by tuber; site where it can colonize freely.
Bold 4-7 ft woodland-edge perennial with deep blue-green angular leaves and flat-topped white flower clusters held atop tall purple stems. Draws pollinators to shade in late summer.

fallColor: yellow sunflowers from midsummer into fall
notes: Distinctive 2-4 ft prairie sunflower with most leaves clustered at the base, leaving slender bare stems topped with airy clusters of yellow daisies. Well-behaved (unusual for native Helianthus): clumping, not running. Thrives in lean dry soil.

Clean clumping 1-3 ft beardtongue with airy branched clusters of small white tube-flowers (faintly streaked purple inside) in early summer. Tolerates dry lean soil and a hard summer. A good Penstemon for tough conditions.

fallColor: flat-topped magenta-purple flower clusters; rust-tan seed heads
notes: 3-5 ft ironweed with broad flat-topped clusters of velvety magenta-purple flowers in late summer that butterflies cannot leave alone. More compact than common Ironweed; tolerates seasonal wet.
2-3 ft woodland-edge perennial with whorls of slender leaves and unusual snowflake-like white flowers with deeply fringed petals. Subtle but very long-blooming through midsummer.

fallColor: upright pyramidal plumes of bright yellow flowers on reddish stems
notes: A native goldenrod grown for its looks: 2-5 ft upright reddish stems topped with dense pyramidal plumes of large bright-yellow flowers. Clump-forming (not running), holds itself well; a good goldenrod for gardens.
1-2 ft spring woodland plant with deeply lobed blue-green foliage and bright 2-inch yellow poppy flowers for weeks. May go summer-dormant in dry shade; self-sows freely into pleasing drifts.

bloom.alt: Whole-plant Wood Poppy clump in deciduous woodland with 15+ large bright yellow 4-petal flowers and deeply lobed blue-green leaves

green.alt: Wood Poppy clump showing the deeply cut blue-green leaves at the base and opposite stem-leaf pair (the species name, diphyllum, means two-leaved) with early yellow buds

maturity.notes: Year 1 is a small rosette of blue-green lobed leaves about 6-8" across that may push a few yellow poppy flowers in April-May. By year 2 it's a full 12-18" clump blooming heavily and setting fuzzy seed pods. The plant goes fully dormant by July, leaving a bare spot until next spring. This is normal, not death, so mark the location and don't plant over it. Let the seed pods drop where they fall; in year 3+ you'll have a self-sown colony filling in moist shaded ground.

notes: Delicate 1-2 ft spring woodlander with rungs of ladder-like compound leaves and airy clusters of sky-blue bell-flowers. Looks best in masses; may go summer-dormant in dry years.

bloom.alt: Loose cluster of pale blue 5-lobed bell flowers of Jacob's Ladder with protruding white pollen-bearing threads

green.alt: Jacob's Ladder ring of leaves at the base showing ladder-like leaves made of paired leaflets in spring woodland

maturity.notes: Year 1 from seed is a small rosette of ladder-like pinnate leaves, often only 4-6 inches tall, with no bloom. Year 2 usually produces the first sky-blue bell clusters in April-May on 8-12 inch stems. By year 3 the clump reaches full 12-18 inch size and starts dropping seedlings nearby. Plants go summer-dormant in dry shade, which is normal, not death. Good to know: it self-sows gently into bare leaf litter, so leave a little open ground around mother plants and you'll have a slowly expanding spring carpet.

notes: 1-2 ft shade perennial with upward-facing tube flowers (scarlet outside, butter-yellow inside) that hummingbirds visit again and again. Slow to establish but long-lived; rarely sold, but worth seeking out.

bloom.alt: Two Indian Pink flowers face-on showing the crimson-red tubular exterior and bright yellow 5-pointed star interior

dormant.alt: Late-season Indian Pink with dried, split-open seed capsules atop the flower stalk and paired leaves still on the stem

maturity.notes: Year 1 is a modest 6-8" clump of glossy paired leaves that usually produces one or two flowering stems with a few red-and-yellow tubes. By year 2 expect a 12" clump with a real flush of bloom in May-June, and by years 3-4 it forms a solid 18-24" mound that can rebloom into July if the spent flower stalks are sheared. Slow to wake up in spring, so don't assume it's dead and dig it up; new shoots often don't emerge until well after surrounding woodland perennials have leafed out.

fallColor: horizontal sprays of tiny white daisies with centers aging yellow to rose
notes: 1-3 ft aster with horizontal sprays of tiny white daisies, each with a center that ages from yellow to rose (the 'calico' effect). One of the latest natives to bloom (often into November); tolerates dry shade.

fallColor: frosted clouds of small white daisies persist past frost
notes: 2-5 ft pioneer aster of disturbed ground, with clouds of small white daisies from late September into November, often persisting after frost. Aggressive self-sower; good for filling tough, wild sites, less so for tidy borders.

fallColor: daisies with drooping yellow petals and domed orange centers
notes: 3-5 ft late-season perennial with golden-yellow daisies whose petals droop like a skirt around a domed orange-yellow center. Likes wet soil, so it suits rain gardens. Common name 'sneezeweed' refers to historic snuff use, not allergies.

fallColor: upright wheat-like seed spikes age to tan and persist
notes: A 2-4 ft clumping grass that grows in spring and fall, with upright wheat-like seed spikes. One of the few native grasses for shade. Green when most summer-growing grasses are dormant; quick to establish from seed.

fallColor: diffuse rosy-purple flower clouds float above foliage; tumbleweeds in fall
notes: Low 1-2 ft clumping grass that grows in summer heat, with airy purple-pink flower clouds in late summer that detach as tumbleweeds in fall. Demands lean, dry, sunny ground.

fallColor: wiry green tufts persist into winter
notes: Tough 1-2 ft tufted rush that thrives in compacted, periodically wet ground, including footpaths and yard edges where lawn fails. Inconspicuous brown summer flowers; valued for resilience, not show.

2-3 ft prairie plant, woody at the base, with silky silver-gray compound leaves and dense purple flower spikes dotted with bright orange pollen tips. Deep tap-root makes it extremely drought-tolerant once established. Best grown from seed.

bloom.alt: Leadplant purple flower spikes with bright orange protruding pollen sacs above silvery-gray foliage of many small leaflets

fall.alt: Amorpha canescens with yellow fall-color pinnate leaves and persistent dark seed spikes standing in prairie

maturity.notes: Notoriously slow above-ground while it builds a deep taproot. Year 1 is just a few silvery seedling stems under 6 inches, year 2 adds modest height, and meaningful purple-and-gold flower spikes usually wait until year 3 or 4. Full 2-3 ft subshrub form with reliable Jun-Jul bloom typically arrives in year 4-6. Good to know: that deep taproot means it resents transplanting. Site it once in lean, well-drained soil in full sun and leave it; mature plants are essentially permanent and fire/mowing-rejuvenated.

fallColor: seed pods turn yellowish brown in late summer to early fall
notes: 6-12 ft suckering shrub of riverbanks and floodplains with airy locust-like compound leaves and dense purple flower spikes dotted with orange pollen tips. Vigorous spreader, so choose its site carefully.

fallColor: long-blooming golden daisies on tall stems; dark seed cones persist
notes: Tall 4-6 ft Rudbeckia with masses of golden daisies for months, far longer-blooming than R. fulgida. Slightly fragrant foliage; dark central cones persist as good winter structure. Tolerates clay and seasonal wet.

fallColor: cloud of small yellow-orange daisies with dark eyes; freely self-sows
notes: Short-lived 2-5 ft Rudbeckia that explodes into a cloud of small yellow-orange daisies with chocolate-brown centers, blooming for months into frost. Self-sows freely; individual plants don't last but a colony does. Tolerates more shade than most Rudbeckia.

Unusual 1-3 ft monarda with stacked tiers of pale-yellow flowers spotted purple, framed by pink-tinged leaves. A major nectar source for many native wasps and bees, humming with insect activity for weeks. Mildew-resistant; needs lean dry soil.

bloom.alt: Whole-plant Spotted Bee Balm bloom in August Wisconsin: the tiered pagoda shape, a ring of cream-yellow purple-spotted tubular flowers framed by lavender-pink leaf-like upper parts, with a soldier beetle visiting and lance-shaped paired leaves below on the square stem.

maturity.notes: Year 1: rosette to small flowering plant, often blooms first year from spring-sown seed; Year 2: the most tiers of pink leaves, may self-sow heavily; often dies after 2-3 years; tolerates poor sandy soil, so avoid rich amendments and irrigation, and let it self-seed into bare patches to maintain a colony.

notes: Drought-loving 2-4 ft vervain with silvery-hairy gray-green leaves and candelabras of slender purple flower spikes that bloom bottom-up for months. The sun-and-dry counterpart of Blue Vervain; thrives on heat.

Tallest of the native Liatris: 3-5 ft slender stems form dense feathery purple bottlebrush spikes that open from the top down. Draws butterflies and hummingbirds; tolerates seasonal wet better than prairie kin.

bloom.alt: Whole-plant Prairie Blazing Star bloom in July Arkansas prairie: multiple tall slender stems with dense feathery magenta bottlebrush spikes blooming top-down, framed by grass-like upright leaves, the densest spike form of the native blazing star species.

green.alt: Pre-bloom Liatris pycnostachya in May Mississippi: dense clump of narrow grass-like basal leaves with multiple stems carrying emerging fuzzy spike-tips, the grass-like vegetative fountain that becomes the 3-5 ft flower spikes.

maturity.notes: Year 1: grassy leaves at the base while it builds its bulb-like root (corm); Year 2: first flowering spike, often shorter than mature height; Year 3: full 3-5 ft spikes with peak bloom; its bulb-like root does best left alone, so avoid dividing it, and stake tall spikes in rich soil to prevent flopping.

fallColor: charcoal-black seed pods rattle through winter
notes: 3-5 ft bold perennial with smooth blue-green pea-family foliage, tall white pea-flower spikes in late spring, and charcoal-black seed pods that rattle into winter. Deep taproot, so site it permanently; ages into a shrub-like presence.

bloom.alt: Dense upright spike of pure white pea-shaped flowers on a dark grey-purple stem against a dark background.

green.alt: Whole-plant mounding shrub-like Baptisia alba var. alba with blue-green trifoliate foliage at the J. C. Raulston Arboretum.

winter.alt: Leaning standing dead skeleton of Baptisia alba with persistent dark grey-black inflated pea pods in winter prairie grasses, Iowa.

maturity.years: Slow to establish; first sparse bloom typically year 2-3 from a container (3-4 yrs from seed), mature 3-4 ft shrub-like clump in 4-5 yrs once the taproot is set
maturity.notes: Drives a deep, woody taproot the first 1-2 years before bulking up above ground. Pick its forever spot and plant young, because established crowns refuse to be divided or moved and resent any spade work near the base.

notes: Low 1-2 ft early-blooming Baptisia with horizontal sprays of creamy-yellow pea-flowers. One of the earliest prairie perennials to flower. Densely hairy gray-green foliage; slow to establish but extremely long-lived.

Compact 2-3 ft Baptisia with delicate three-part clover-like leaves and airy sprays of small bright-yellow pea-flowers through early summer. The most drought-adapted Baptisia; thrives in lean sandy soil.
